question: A 4-year-old child has been seizing for 8 minutes and IV access is now established. Blood glucose is 5.2 mmol/L. Which of the following is the CORRECT next immediate step?

answers.text: IV phenytoin 20 mg/kg in dextrose-containing solution, infused over 20 minutes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Phenytoin is a second-line agent for status epilepticus, not the immediate first step after IV access. Critically, phenytoin must NEVER be infused in a dextrose-containing solution — it precipitates. It should be given in normal saline. Lorazepam is the first-line agent when IV access is available.

answers.text: IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg), given over 2 minutes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. With IV access available after 5–10 minutes of seizure, IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (max 4 mg) is the first-line benzodiazepine. Blood glucose has been checked and is normal. Phenytoin (20 mg/kg in normal saline — NOT dextrose) is reserved for seizures that persist despite two benzodiazepine doses. Lorazepam has a longer duration of action than diazepam for sustained seizure control.

answers.text: IV midazolam 0.2 mg/kg, then prepare for immediate intubation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Midazolam (IV or buccal) is an alternative benzodiazepine when lorazepam is unavailable, but immediate intubation is not indicated at this stage — pharmacological seizure control should be attempted first through the stepwise protocol before progressing to anaesthetic agents for refractory SE.

answers.text: PR diazepam 0.5 mg/kg, as it provides faster onset than IV lorazepam

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Rectal diazepam is used when no IV access is available (community or pre-hospital setting). Since IV access is now established, IV lorazepam is preferred — it has more predictable pharmacokinetics and a longer duration of seizure suppression than rectal diazepam. PR diazepam does NOT have faster onset than IV lorazepam when IV access is available.

overallFeedback.feedback: With established IV access: lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV is the first-line agent. Key trap: phenytoin must NEVER be mixed in dextrose — it precipitates. PR diazepam is reserved for when IV access is unavailable. Always check blood glucose before anticonvulsants.

Correct. With IV access: lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg) is first-line. Always check glucose first. Phenytoin (second-line, in normal saline NOT dextrose) is for persistent SE after two benzodiazepine doses.
